transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Hi, doctor. Nice to meet you. 

Well, what brings me in is that I just keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put. I'm a private investigator, and it happens a lot during client interviews. I'll just stand up and start pacing. It happens outside of work, too, like during tutoring sessions or even at my book club. 

People are really starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen, and it's becoming an issue for me, so I figured I needed to come talk to someone about it.

When you're pacing or standing up during these situations, are you having trouble focusing on what the other person is saying, or is it more that your body just needs to move even though you want to listen?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. I guess I haven't paid close attention to exactly why it happens in the moment. 

I just know I'll be sitting there, and then... I just feel like I have to get up. I don't really know if I'm losing focus on what they're saying or if my body just refuses to stay in the chair. I just know I always end up on my feet.

When you feel that urge to get up and start pacing, do you experience an uncomfortable feeling inside—like a restless tension or an urge that you have to act on—or does it feel more like your mind is just wandering and you naturally want to move around?

I guess I don't really know how to describe the feeling inside. I haven't really thought about whether it's a restless tension or just my mind wandering. I just know that I can't stay seated. I haven't really noticed what exactly is going on in my head or my body right before I stand up. I just do it.

When you get that urge to stand up and pace, do you feel something physically uncomfortable inside your body—like a tension or an itch in your muscles or a restless feeling that makes you need to move—or does it feel more like your thoughts are just pulling you away from sitting?

I honestly don't know how to break it down like that. It's not like I feel an itch or a specific tension in my muscles... and I wouldn't say my thoughts are pulling me away, either. It's just a general feeling of needing to not be sitting anymore. I'm sorry, I know you're trying to get a specific answer, but I just haven't analyzed it that closely. I just know I end up walking around.
How long has this problem with not being able to stay seated been going on? Has it always been like this for you, or did it start at a particular time?

Well, I've always been a bit antsy, I guess, but it's been noticeably worse for about eight months now. That's when I had to move out of my old apartment in Chicago. Ever since then, it just seems a lot harder to stay put.
When you moved out of your apartment in Chicago eight months ago, was that move stressful or difficult for you? What was going on at that time?

I mean, moving is always a bit of a hassle, just dealing with boxes and logistics. But... no, it wasn't particularly difficult or stressful. Nothing major was going on in my life. My lease was just up, so I found a new place. I really don't know why it got so much harder to sit still around that time. It just sort of... happened, I guess.

When you're doing something you really enjoy or find interesting—like working on a case as a private investigator—are you able to sit still and concentrate, or do you find yourself getting up and pacing even then?

I haven't really noticed if there's a difference, to be honest. When I'm deep into a case... well, I'm not entirely sure if I stay seated longer just because it's interesting. I haven't really paid attention to it like that. I just know I'm up and down a lot during the day, pretty much no matter what I'm working on.

When you feel that need to get up and pace, if you tried very hard to stay seated—say, if your job depended on it—do you think you could force yourself to stay in the chair, or does it feel like something you literally cannot control no matter how hard you try?

I mean... I don't really know. I guess I've never been in a situation where I absolutely, 100 percent couldn't get up. I just feel this... this really strong urge to move, and it's so uncomfortable to fight it. I don't know if I could force myself to stay seated if my job depended on it. I just haven't tried to push it that far.

When you get that urge to stand up and pace, would you say there's an uncomfortable feeling inside—like an inner agitation or restlessness—that makes you want to move, or is it more that you just don't feel like sitting and your body naturally wants to be active?

I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be honest. I guess I haven't really paid attention to whether it's an inner agitation or just my body wanting to be active. It's hard to separate the two. I just... I just know that sitting still starts to feel wrong after a while, so I get up. I couldn't really say which one of those it is.

When you're sitting still and feel that urge to get up, would you describe the feeling as actively uncomfortable or distressing—something that bothers you and makes you want to escape it—or is it more that sitting just doesn't feel natural to you and moving feels better?

I don't really know how to describe it, honestly. It's not like... it's not like a sharp pain or something that actively hurts. But it's also not just that moving feels better. I guess I haven't really thought about whether it's distressing or just unnatural. It's just... I get this feeling, and I have to move. I don't know if I can put it into either of those categories.

When you're sitting and get that urge to move, does it feel like there's something inside you that's bothering you or making you uncomfortable—like you need to escape that feeling by moving—or does it feel more like your body just naturally wants to be in motion, without any sense that sitting is actually bothering you?

I... I really don't know how else to explain it. I feel like you're asking the same question again, and I just don't have a clear answer for it. I haven't analyzed it that deeply. I just sit, I get the urge to move, and I get up. I don't know if it's an inner bother or just my body wanting motion. It's just what happens.

If you were completely paralyzed from the neck down but still awake and aware, would you feel a strong inner discomfort or agitation that makes you want to move—even though you couldn't—or would you just feel fine sitting still since your body wouldn't be able to move anyway?

I... wow, that's an extreme example. I honestly don't know how I'd feel in that situation. I've never been paralyzed, so I can't really guess if I'd feel agitated inside or if I'd just be fine. I mean, my brain would probably still be going a million miles an hour, but as for the physical urge to move? I just don't know. I can't really imagine what that would feel like.

When you get that urge to stand up and pace, if you were forced to stay seated for 10 minutes, would you feel anxious, irritable, or emotionally distressed—like something is wrong or bothering you—or would you just be bored or restless without that emotional upset?

I think... if I had to sit there for ten minutes and absolutely couldn't get up, I’d probably just feel really restless. Like, my leg would start bouncing, I'd be shifting around in the chair, maybe tapping my fingers. I don't think I'd feel anxious or emotionally upset, like something was terribly wrong. I'd just be really antsy and bored, waiting for the ten minutes to be up so I could finally move.

When you're sitting and get that urge to move, if you compare it to times when you're bored or waiting in line, is the feeling the same kind of restlessness, or does this urge to move feel like something different—something more internal or harder to ignore?

I think it's just the same kind of restlessness. Like if I'm stuck waiting in line at the grocery store, I'm shifting my weight, looking around, maybe checking my phone, just wanting things to move along. When I'm sitting and get the urge to get up, it feels pretty much like that. It doesn't feel like some deep, internal... thing that's totally different. It's just that same basic feeling of wanting to be doing something else, or just wanting to be in motion.

When you're trying to focus on something—like reading a case file or listening to someone speak—do you find your mind wandering or getting distracted easily, or are you able to concentrate on what you're doing even though your body wants to move around?

I can usually concentrate pretty well. I mean, my body might be doing its own thing—like I said, my leg bouncing or me shifting in my seat—but my mind is on the job. If I'm reading a file or listening to a client, I'm focused on what they're saying or what's on the page. I don't really have a problem with my mind wandering off. It's more just the physical need to be moving while I'm doing it.

You mentioned you can usually concentrate well on your work. But when you're reading case files or listening to someone speak, do you ever find it hard to keep your attention on what they're saying, or do you sometimes miss details because your mind drifted to something else?

No, not really. Like I was just saying, I don't really have an issue with my mind drifting off. In my line of work, missing details isn't really an option anyway. So, no, I don't find it hard to keep my attention on what someone is saying or what I'm reading. I stay focused on the information, it's just my body that wants to keep moving while I do it.

When you're at your book club or in tutoring sessions, do you ever have trouble keeping up with what's being discussed because your mind wanders, or do you follow along fine even though your body is restless?

No, I follow along fine. It's the same thing as with work—I don't really have trouble keeping up with the discussion. My mind stays on the book or whatever we're talking about in the tutoring session. I might be shifting around in my chair or tapping my foot, but I'm paying attention to what everyone is saying. I don't really space out or miss things.

When you're doing something that's not very interesting to you—like waiting in a doctor's office or sitting through a boring meeting—do you find it harder to pay attention, or do you still focus just fine even if your body is restless?

No, I still focus fine. Even if it's boring, I don't really have a problem paying attention to what's going on. I mean, I might be annoyed that I'm stuck waiting or sitting through something dull, and I'll definitely be fidgeting or wanting to get up and leave, but my mind doesn't wander off. I'm still present and aware of what's happening around me.
When you were a kid in elementary school or middle school, do you remember being restless or fidgety back then, or is this something that only really started happening as an adult?

Oh, no, it's always been this way. Even back in elementary school. I mean, my old report cards... they always said I was bright, but that I just couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother still jokes about it, actually. She tells people I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. So, no, it definitely didn't just start as an adult.

Like, my leg would start bouncing, I'd be shifting around in the chair, maybe tapping my fingers. I don't think I'd feel anxious or emotionally upset, like something was terribly wrong. I'd just be really antsy and bored, waiting for the ten minutes to be up so I could finally move.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences akathisia (an inner sense of restlessness/agitation that is qualitatively different from simple fidgetiness) versus pure motor restlessness/hyperactivity, which would help differentiate G25.81 (Restlessness, unspecified) from ADHD presentations
doctor.question: When you're sitting and get that urge to move, if you compare it to times when you're bored or waiting in line, is the feeling the same kind of restlessness, or does this urge to move feel like something different—something more internal or harder to ignore?

target_item.reason: The doctor is still asking about the subjective experience of the urge to move (whether it feels like boredom/restlessness or something different/more internal). None of the symptom profile items directly address this specific qualitative description of the internal urge.

patient.answer: I think it's just the same kind of restlessness. Like if I'm stuck waiting in line at the grocery store, I'm shifting my weight, looking around, maybe checking my phone, just wanting things to move along. When I'm sitting and get the urge to get up, it feels pretty much like that. It doesn't feel like some deep, internal... thing that's totally different. It's just that same basic feeling of wanting to be doing something else, or just wanting to be in motion.

inference.note: Ruled out G25.81 (Restless Legs Syndrome) - patient denies uncomfortable physical sensations, tension, or inner agitation; describes simple restlessness and boredom similar to waiting in line, not the characteristic dysphoria of RLS. Ruled out F90.1 and F90.2 - patient is an adult with no clear evidence of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms meeting ADHD criteria; symptoms are nonspecific restlessness without cognitive impairment. Narrowed to F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) as the most consistent with lifelong 'antsy' baseline and worsening restlessness, though presentation remains atypical.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had symptoms of inattention, distractibility, or difficulty sustaining attention—core features of ADHD that would distinguish it from simple restlessness or akathisia
doctor.question: When you're trying to focus on something—like reading a case file or listening to someone speak—do you find your mind wandering or getting distracted easily, or are you able to concentrate on what you're doing even though your body wants to move around?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about inattention symptoms (mind wandering, getting distracted easily), which are characteristic of the Predominantly Inattentive Presentation of ADHD. My symptom profile only includes hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, so I do not have a specific symptom to report for inattention.

patient.answer: I can usually concentrate pretty well. I mean, my body might be doing its own thing—like I said, my leg bouncing or me shifting in my seat—but my mind is on the job. If I'm reading a file or listening to a client, I'm focused on what they're saying or what's on the page. I don't really have a problem with my mind wandering off. It's more just the physical need to be moving while I'm doing it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has symptoms of inattention/distractibility that would support ADHD diagnosis, since they've reported good concentration despite physical restlessness
doctor.question: You mentioned you can usually concentrate well on your work. But when you're reading case files or listening to someone speak, do you ever find it hard to keep your attention on what they're saying, or do you sometimes miss details because your mind drifted to something else?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of inattention, specifically difficulty sustaining attention or mind wandering (missing details because the mind drifted). My symptom profile is for Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation and does not include inattentive symptoms like difficulty sustaining attention (S002) or not listening (S003). Therefore, I should return None.

patient.answer: No, not really. Like I was just saying, I don't really have an issue with my mind drifting off. In my line of work, missing details isn't really an option anyway. So, no, I don't find it hard to keep my attention on what someone is saying or what I'm reading. I stay focused on the information, it's just my body that wants to keep moving while I do it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has significant inattention symptoms or only the hyperactivity/restlessness component, which would help differentiate between ADHD presentations or confirm if this is primarily a hyperactivity-only presentation
doctor.question: When you're at your book club or in tutoring sessions, do you ever have trouble keeping up with what's being discussed because your mind wanders, or do you follow along fine even though your body is restless?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about inattention (trouble keeping up with discussions, mind wandering) at book club or tutoring sessions. My symptom profile is predominantly hyperactive/impulsive and does not include inattention symptoms, so I do not have a specific symptom to match this.

patient.answer: No, I follow along fine. It's the same thing as with work—I don't really have trouble keeping up with the discussion. My mind stays on the book or whatever we're talking about in the tutoring session. I might be shifting around in my chair or tapping my foot, but I'm paying attention to what everyone is saying. I don't really space out or miss things.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has symptoms of inattention or distractibility that would support ADHD diagnosis, since they've consistently denied mind-wandering and concentration problems despite acknowledging significant motor restlessness.
doctor.question: When you're doing something that's not very interesting to you—like waiting in a doctor's office or sitting through a boring meeting—do you find it harder to pay attention, or do you still focus just fine even if your body is restless?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining attention in uninteresting situations (inattention symptom). This is not covered in my profile, which only includes hyperactive/impulsive symptoms.

patient.answer: No, I still focus fine. Even if it's boring, I don't really have a problem paying attention to what's going on. I mean, I might be annoyed that I'm stuck waiting or sitting through something dull, and I'll definitely be fidgeting or wanting to get up and leave, but my mind doesn't wander off. I'm still present and aware of what's happening around me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had symptoms of hyperactivity/restlessness since childhood or early adolescence, which would be necessary for an ADHD diagnosis, versus this being a purely adult-onset condition
doctor.question: When you were a kid in elementary school or middle school, do you remember being restless or fidgety back then, or is this something that only really started happening as an adult?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My grade-school report cards always said I was bright but couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn, and my mother still jokes that I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the patient was restless or fidgety as a child in elementary or middle school, which directly relates to the onset of symptoms prior to age 12 years.

patient.answer: Oh, no, it's always been this way. Even back in elementary school. I mean, my old report cards... they always said I was bright, but that I just couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother still jokes about it, actually. She tells people I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. So, no, it definitely didn't just start as an adult.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with lifelong hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (restlessness, inability to remain seated, fidgeting) dating back to elementary school, with recent exacerbation over 8 months. While attention and concentration remain intact, the persistent motor restlessness across multiple settings (work, social, educational) and the childhood onset are consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation. The symptom pattern does not meet criteria for a specific anxiety or adjustment disorder, and functional impairment is present in social and professional contexts.
